basis: All six evidence commands re-run and produce the stated output. The two subject files are byte-identical between the declared baseline 740976ec and the worktree HEAD bcfa9f33 (`git diff --stat 740976ec..HEAD -- internal/adapters/clients/azureai/ internal/domain/ai/ cmd/slabledger/` is empty), so verifying at HEAD verifies at baseline. I then re-derived the claim by a stronger, type-aware route than the finding used. (A) COMPILE PROOF. I exported the tree with `git archive HEAD | tar -x -C /tmp/deadgo002` (a scratch copy outside the repo; the repo was not modified), confirmed the unmodified copy builds, then deleted exactly the two blast_radius files. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go vet -tags integration ./...`, and `go test -run ZZZNONEXISTENT ./...` (which compiles every test binary in the module) all succeed with zero diagnostics. `go test ./...` then exits 0 across 49 packages with no FAIL and no panic. A Go compiler resolving the whole module reports no dependency on ai.ImageGenerator, ai.ImageRequest, ai.ImageResult, azureai.ImageClient, ImageOption, NewImageClient, WithImageLogger, or GenerateImage. This is type-aware, so unlike the textual map it does see interface satisfaction, embedding, unexported identifiers, and inline interface method sets — the exact blind spots LENS-BRIEF §2 caveat 4 warns about. (B) INTERFACE VALUE, held or called through. `git grep -nE '\bImageGenerator\b' -- '*.go'` returns four lines and only four: internal/domain/ai/image.go:5 (doc comment) and :6 (the type declaration), and internal/adapters/clients/azureai/image_client.go:24 (doc comment) and :61 (`var _ ai.ImageGenerator = (*ImageClient)(nil)`). The interface is never named as a struct field type, a function parameter, or a return type anywhere in the tree, so no interface value of that type is ever held. Independently, `git grep -n 'GenerateImage' -- '*.go'` (deliberately unanchored, so it also catches the method name appearing inside a string literal for reflection or string-keyed dispatch) returns three lines: image_client.go:79 (doc comment), image_client.go:82 (the method definition), and image.go:7 (the interface method declaration). Zero call sites. A method set that is never invoked cannot be reached through an interface value, so the assertion at :61 hides nothing — consistent with the dispatch note that the assertion alone proves nothing in either direction. (C) DEPENDENCY INJECTION, including nil-but-declared. `git grep -nE '\bai\.' -- 'cmd/**/*.go'` returns exactly one line tree-wide, cmd/slabledger/handlers.go:228 (`var aiTracker ai.AICallTracker`), an unrelated symbol. The sole import of the azureai package is cmd/slabledger/init_services.go:14, and the sole use is init_services.go:66 constructing `azureai.NewClient` (the text/LLM client) with `azureai.WithLogger` and `azureai.WithCompletionTimeout`. No constructor, scheduler builder, router, or functional option anywhere accepts an ai.ImageGenerator, so this is an absent dependency rather than a nil-but-declared one, and the distinction does not change the finding. `git grep -niE 'image|generate' -- 'internal/adapters/httpserver/routes*.go'` is empty (no endpoint) and `git grep -rniE 'generate.?image|image.?generat' -- 'web/src'` is empty (no frontend caller). (D) CONFIG GATING. There is no image-generation config plumbing, so the fix unit is NOT larger than the two types on the config axis. azureai.Config (client.go:24-29) is a single shared struct — Endpoint, APIKey, DeploymentName, APIVersion — used by both clients; NewImageClient takes that same type and adds no field of its own. The tracked env surface is AZURE_AI_ENDPOINT, AZURE_AI_API_KEY, AZURE_AI_DEPLOYMENT, AZURE_AI_TIMEOUT (names only, read from the tracked .env.example and internal/platform/config/loader.go:184-192; no real .env file was opened). Every one is consumed by the live LLM client at init_services.go:66, and AZURE_AI_DEPLOYMENT defaults to a text model ("gpt-5.4", loader.go:188) — there is no separate image deployment or endpoint variable to orphan. `git grep -rniE 'dall.?e|image_deployment|IMAGE_DEPLOYMENT|imagegen|image_gen'` returns no hit under internal/, cmd/, web/, or .env.example. (E) SAME-NAME COLLISION ruled out. A tree-wide `git grep -niE '\bimage' -- '*.go'` with the two subject files excluded returns roughly 90 lines, and every one is an unrelated domain: PSA slab photo URLs, DH card image_url columns, Shopify import image columns, cardladder thumbnails, and Docker container-image prose. None is AI image generation, so nothing in that noise makes the cluster look live. (F) The finding's own reasoning, read last, matches what I found; all nine runtime_checks are answered and each is accurate against my re-derivation.
what_the_finding_got_wrong: One real gap, in scope rather than in the central claim: blast_radius lists only the two .go files, but the cluster also has two live documentation references that the deletion must reconcile — docs/LLM_USAGE.md:53, which reproduces the ImageGenerator interface body verbatim under 'Domain interface', and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:68 and :264, where the interface table carries the row `| ai | ImageGenerator | llm.go | 1 | Image generation |`. I confirmed this bites: after deleting only the two blast_radius files in the scratch copy, a grep for the seven symbol names over docs/, internal/, cmd/, and web/ (excluding docs/audit/ itself) still returns docs/LLM_USAGE.md and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md. So acceptance_criteria #2 ('git grep for ImageGenerator, ImageClient, ... returns no results'), which is not scoped to '*.go', cannot be satisfied by the stated blast_radius alone. The criterion is not wrong — it correctly forces the fixer to the docs — but blast_radius understates the fix by two files, and the ticket should name them. Separately, that ARCHITECTURE.md row misattributes the interface to llm.go when it is declared in image.go; the row is being deleted anyway, so this only matters as a hint that the doc was already stale. Neither point disturbs the central claim, and I found nothing that would justify lowering severity: the cluster is documented in two places as though it were a live capability, which is precisely the kind of misdirection a medium-severity dead-code finding is for.
